title: Short Stuff: RICO Act
summary: Short Stuff episode explaining the RICO Act (Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act). The hosts open with banter about mob boss John Gotti ("Teflon Don") and the mafia films that reference RICO, then explain that RICO targets people who direct or manage an illegal enterprise rather than the hands-on perpetrators. They cover the two-part proof required (a pattern of racketeering activity and proof the defendant directed the enterprise), how Gotti was convicted using informant Sammy "the Bull" Gravano's testimony and wiretaps, and how the act was later used in civil suits, including a 2015 Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal case and a civil suit against the Catholic Church. A brief ad break for iHeartRadio appears mid-episode, and the episode closes with a sign-off.
topics: Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act

segments.title: Opening banter and John Gotti
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Halloween costumes and John Gotti, the Teflon Don, and introduce the RICO Act as the law that eventually took him down.

segments.title: What the RICO Act stands for
segments.summary: The hosts explain the acronym Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act, define racket and racketeering, and argue the name is confusing compared with a plain organized crime act. They note RICO has been applied to white collar and corporate crime as well as mob enterprises.

segments.title: How RICO targets leaders and the two-part proof
segments.summary: RICO aims at high-level managers who direct illegal enterprises but do not personally commit the crimes. Prosecutors must prove a pattern of racketeering activity and that the defendant directed the enterprise. Federal prosecutors use it when other charges are not enough.

segments.title: Gotti's conviction and civil RICO suits
segments.summary: Gotti was convicted using informant Sammy the Bull Gravano's testimony and wiretap recordings of Gotti issuing orders. Gotti died in prison. The hosts discuss civil RICO suits with triple damages, the later four-year statute of limitations, and a civil suit against the Catholic Church, plus the 2015 Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal case.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up with jokes and the standard Short Stuff sign-off.
